From vars.sas to R: study-build and variable actions

John Ehrlinger

2026-10-23

Source: vignettes/articles/vars-sas-to-r.qmd

Who this is for

This guide is for a biostatistician or statistical programmer who has worked inside a SAS study’s vars.sas. You know the two lines every analysis job opens with,

%inc vars;
%vars(impute=0, missing=1, propen=0, match=0, transf=1);

and you have probably edited a vars.sas that someone copied from the last study. The R side takes the work that program does apart into single-purpose actions. This guide shows where each piece of vars.sas (and of bd.*.sas) now lives, what a study’s R code looks like, and why some of the choices that will feel strange were made on purpose.

A design, not yet a package

This article describes the design in dev/specs/2026-10-14-bd-vars-action-items-design.md. None of the new functions exist yet. Their names (recode(), missing_flags(), join_artifact() and the rest) are working names that will settle when the pieces are built, and every code chunk below is illustrative and is not run. read_job_data() exists today; its vars argument does not. Where this article and the spec disagree, the spec wins.

What vars.sas does today

It helps to say plainly what the program is before taking it apart.

vars.sas is not a build step. Its header calls it the “macro to bring in variables for analysis”, and that is what it does: each analysis job runs %vars(...), the macro recomputes everything, and nothing is saved. Its arguments are already a switchboard of modules. IMPUTE= turns on informative imputing (a missing value set to a stated constant), MISSING= the mean fill, PROPEN= and MATCH= merge a score or a match indicator that another job wrote, and TRANSF= the log, inverse and square transforms. Around those switches sit the recodes, the age dichotomies, the dummy columns, the missing-value indicators, the %let variable lists and, in many studies, value fixes and patient deletions that do not belong there.

So the modules exist in spirit. They are knotted into one macro of about 900 lines that each study copies and edits, and the copies drift. In one sampled study, a coronary indicator is set to 10 where its three siblings are set to 1, and the mitral and tricuspid stenosis-severity fills test the aortic severity’s missingness, a copy-paste of the aortic line. Neither defect would survive a test of a single action. Both survived a 900-line file.

There is one more place %vars runs that is easy to forget. bd.SAStoR.sas, the bridge that writes the XPORT file R reads, runs %vars with its defaults and then keeps a hand-picked column list. Every legacy study already in R therefore carries SAS vars output inside its dataset, and that keep list is the study’s de facto variable list. We come back to this under adopted studies.

The one rule the new design keeps

Everything below follows from a boundary that was set at the 2026-10-14 training:

  • The study build (bd) queries, joins, corrects, sets the cohort and computes the standard derivations. It writes built.
  • A job may filter rows and drop columns. It never corrects a value.
  • Multiple imputation, balancing scores and matching are their own jobs, not switches.

The design then gives every verb a home, in one of three places. B actions are sections of the one bd job. V actions are small functions your study’s vars() calls. J actions are jobs of their own that save a small artifact keyed by patient. The picture shows how the data moves between them.

Where everything went

Read this table from the left: find the SAS piece you know, and the right-hand columns say where it lives now.

In SAS today Action Lives in What it does
recode blocks in vars.sas V1 recode a vars function a categorical recode
age and other cut-points V2 dichotomize a vars function cut-points or groupings into a new column
dummy NYHA and the like V3 dummies a vars function indicator columns from a categorical
%inc tp.vars.<umbrella> V4 rule a vars function, driven by rule rows in a private repository a derivation that differs by study or umbrella
TRANSF=, %ln, %inv V5 transform a vars function log, inverse and square, with their scale constants
the flag block V6 missing flags a vars function, on the whole built indicators by the 5 to 30% rule
MISSING=, proc standard replace V7 screening fill a vars function, on the whole built mean fill for screening only, with the means recorded
%let lists, SAStoR’s keep V8 variable sets data in the study’s R/ named variable lists for analyses
IMPUTE=, if x = . then x = <constant> V9 informative fill a vars function a missing value set to a stated constant, recorded per column
proc mi, tp.bd.mult.imput J1 impute its own job (mi) m completed datasets, keyed and seeded
PROPEN= J2 balancing score its own job (lm-propensity_*, rm-balancing_continuous) id → score
MATCH=, tp.bd.*match* J3 match its own job; prefix not yet chosen id → match id
if ccfid = ... then inside vars B3 correct the study overlay, applied by bd one corrected cell, with its evidence
if ... then delete inside vars B4 cohort bd for the study population; WHERE in a job removes rows, with a reason and a count
proc print, proc means diagnostics a dt job, or bd’s report prints and summaries of intermediate data

One switch name misleads. IMPUTE= is not multiple imputation. It sets a missing value to a stated constant, which is a vars function (V9). Multiple imputation is J1, a job of its own, and in SAS it already lived in separate programs.

The bd.*.sas program breaks into sections the same way:

Section Does In SAS today
B0 adopt registers a legacy SAStoR dataset, recording that SAS applied vars and the keep list bd.SAStoR.sas
B1 cut reads the corrected base, pinned with as_of set modules.bd*_&PULLDT
B2 join attaches a source by key; a windowed join (the latest pre-operative lab before the operation) is a named kind merge, proc sql, lab programs
B3 correct applies the study overlay’s cells if ccfid = ... then
B4 cohort removes rows, each rule with a reason and a count if ... then delete
B5 derive intervals, age, BSA, from the master’s own definitions scattered through bd
B6 select keeps or drops columns keep, drop
B7 register writes built and registers a dated version nothing

Three checks follow from the tables, and later each becomes a test. bd never recodes or transforms. vars never filters rows and never corrects a value. A J job never writes into built.

A study’s R/vars.R

In SAS, vars.sas sits in the study and every job includes it. The R equivalent is a file in the study’s R/ folder, which .job_setup() already sources at the top of every job. It defines one function, vars(), that takes the data and returns it, and it reads as a pipe of the primitives that hvtiRdatabuild will provide.

# R/vars.R: the study's variable actions. Illustrative; the primitives are working names.

# EDIT: the umbrellas whose rules this study uses. Each name is a set of rule rows in the
# private rules repository, the R home of what tp.vars.<umbrella> holds today.
UMBRELLAS <- c("valve")
RULES     <- read_rules(UMBRELLAS)                    # V4, read once per job; see the next section

vars <- function(d) {
  d |>
    hvtiRdatabuild::recode("nyha", c("1" = "I-II", "2" = "I-II", "3" = "III-IV", "4" = "III-IV"),
                           into = "nyha_grp") |>      # V1
    hvtiRdatabuild::dichotomize("age", at = 70, into = "age_ge70") |>  # V2
    hvtiRdatabuild::dummies("nyha") |>                # V3
    apply_rules(RULES) |>                             # V4
    hvtiRdatabuild::transform_ln("age") |>            # V5, writes age_ln
    hvtiRdatabuild::transform_inv("creat") |>         # V5
    hvtiRdatabuild::missing_flags(c("lvef", "creat"), rule = c(0.05, 0.30)) |>  # V6
    hvtiRdatabuild::informative_fill("hx_smoke", value = 0)                    # V9; the spec names no primitive yet
}

# V7 is for screening only, so it is not in vars(), which every job runs. A screening job
# adds it to its own call: vars = function(d) d |> vars() |> hvtiRdatabuild::screening_fill(...)

# V8: named variable sets, data rather than a function. The adoption job records the
# SAStoR keep list as a legacy study's first set.
VARIABLE_SETS <- list(
  baseline = c("age", "sex", "nyha_grp", "lvef", "creat"),
  screen   = c("age_ln", "creat_inv", "lvef", "lvef_miss")
)

The EDIT: marker above differs from one in a job in one respect. Today’s marker guard reads the job file only, so a marker left in the study’s R/ does not stop a final render. Whether study-level choices get a guard of their own is for the sub-project that builds the vars hook to settle.

Each line is one action you can read on its own, and each primitive attaches an action record: what it did, its inputs and outputs, how many values it set and, for the aggregate actions (V6, V7), the statistics it used. Those records print in the report’s “About this run” table, so the means a screening fill used are on the page rather than in a SAS log.

Nothing here is written to disk. That is the same behavior as %vars: every job recomputes, and the study keeps one definition.

Umbrella rules from the private repository

tp.vars.aorta, tp.vars.cabg and their siblings exist because some derivations differ by umbrella. Regurgitation across sources may be the maximum in one umbrella and taken by echo priority in another. Pre-operative atrial fibrillation may blank post-operative atrial fibrillation. A mitral cleanup must not run in an aorta study.

The design splits each of those into mechanism and policy. The mechanism is a generic, tested primitive in hvtiRdatabuild: max_across(), coalesce_by_priority(), set_missing_if(). The policy, which primitive applies to which columns for which umbrella, is a rule row: the umbrella, the output column, the primitive, its inputs and arguments, an owner and a date. The rows are kept in a private Azure DevOps repository, checked out read-only under /programs/development/ on the share so jobs read them directly. An umbrella is the set of rows that share its name.

# Illustrative. The spec names neither function, nor the repository's path (it is open).
read_rules <- function(umbrellas) {
  rows <- utils::read.csv("/programs/development/<rules-repository>/rules.csv")
  rows[rows$umbrella %in% umbrellas, ]
}
# apply_rules(d, rules) calls the primitive each row names, on that row's columns.

A job records the rules file’s commit and SHA-256 in its provenance, the same way it records the overlay’s, so a report can say exactly which rules it ran under. Because the rows are data and not code, moving them into a database table later changes where they are read from and nothing about what they say.

A job that uses vars

read_job_data() will gain a vars argument. You pass it the function, and the shared data step runs it after the read and before WHERE:

# In a job's edit-study-choices chunk, as today:
DATASET      <- "study"
ANALYSIS_SET <- NULL
WHERE        <- quote(age >= 18)
ID           <- "ccfid"

# The data step, with the new argument. vars() came from the study's R/vars.R.
job_data <- hvtiRtemplates::read_job_data(.cfg, dataset = DATASET, analysis_set = ANALYSIS_SET,
                                          where = WHERE, id = ID, vars = vars)
d <- job_data$data

The order matters, and it is the SAS order: %vars, then the job’s subset. A row-wise action such as a recode gives the same value whichever way round you run it. An aggregate does not. The missing-indicator rule and the screening means are computed on the whole built, and the job then keeps its rows. That is what makes the R numbers reconcile with the SAS jobs being ported (see why the whole built).

Joining a balancing score or a match

In SAS, PROPEN=1 merges a score that another job left in a dataset. In R, the balancing score job (lm-propensity_binary and its siblings, or rm-balancing_continuous) writes a small parquet keyed by patient, id → score, registered with the built version it was fitted on. A match job writes id → match id the same way. An analysis job joins one after the read:

# Illustrative: join_artifact() is a working name.
d <- job_data$data |>
  join_artifact("propen")      # adds the score column, by ID

join_artifact() stops if the artifact was fitted on a different built version than the one the job read. A score fitted to last month’s cohort is wrong for this month’s, and nothing in the joined data would look wrong. In SAS nothing checks for that mismatch; here it is a stop with a message naming both versions.

Skipping actions a job does not need

%vars lets a job turn modules off through its switches. A job that fits on raw scale has no use for the transforms, and a descriptive table may want no missing flags at all.

How an R job does this is not decided yet. The spec does not define per-job skipping. Three shapes are on the table, and the choice will be recorded in the spec once it is made.

1. Named pieces the job composes. The study’s R/vars.R defines the pieces separately, and a job pipes together the ones it wants.

vars_base       <- function(d) d |> hvtiRdatabuild::recode(...) |> apply_rules(RULES)
vars_transforms <- function(d) d |> hvtiRdatabuild::transform_ln("age")
vars_missing    <- function(d) d |> hvtiRdatabuild::missing_flags(c("lvef", "creat"))
vars            <- function(d) d |> vars_base() |> vars_transforms() |> vars_missing()

# A job that skips the transforms:
read_job_data(.cfg, where = WHERE, vars = function(d) d |> vars_base() |> vars_missing())

Each piece can be read and tested on its own, and vars() holds no switches. A job’s call names what runs, rather than what doesn’t.

2. A skip argument on the composite. Closest to the %vars switches you know.

read_job_data(.cfg, where = WHERE, vars = function(d) vars(d, skip = "transforms"))

vars() then carries the branching itself, and the step names ("transforms", "missing") become an interface every job depends on.

3. All or nothing. A job runs the study’s whole vars(), or passes vars = NULL and runs none of it. Anything finer is written into the job.

Two things hold whichever shape is chosen. Whatever runs still runs before WHERE, so a skipped action changes which columns a job sees and never how the remaining aggregates are computed. And skipping does not remove a column that is already in the data, which matters for the adopted studies below.

The conversations

These are the objections we expect from people who have spent years in vars.sas. Each one has a reason behind it.

Why are the aggregates computed on the whole built?

Because that is what SAS does today, and the first job of the R port is to give the same numbers. %vars runs before the job subsets, so the 5 to 30% missing-indicator rule and the screening means see every row in built. Computing them on each job’s cohort was considered and not chosen: it would move numbers relative to the SAS jobs being ported, and it would let one study define lvef_miss one way in one job and another way in the next, since each job keeps different rows. On the whole built, a study has one definition per variable.

Why can’t I fix a value in vars?

You can still fix it, just not there. A value fix inside vars.sas is invisible: nobody outside the study learns of it, every job silently re-applies it, and a copy of vars.sas carries it into the next study whether it applies or not. In the new design a correction is one cell in the study’s overlay: the key, the variable, the value expected before, the new value, and the evidence. bd applies it, checks that the prior value still holds, recomputes the derivations from the corrected cell, and proposes it upstream, so another study receives it on its next cut once it is accepted. The same goes for patient removals, which become cohort rules in bd (each with a reason and a count) or a WHERE in the one job that needs it.

Why are imputation, balancing scores and matching their own jobs?

Because each is a fitted model with a seed, and its output should be produced once, looked at, and then reused. SAS already keeps them apart in part. Multiple imputation lives in its own programs (proc mi, tp.bd.mult.imput), and PROPEN= and MATCH= merge a dataset another job wrote. That is the right idea, but nothing ties that dataset to the version of built it was fitted on. (Despite its name, IMPUTE= is not multiple imputation. It sets a missing value to a stated constant, and stays a vars function, V9.) As a job, each is seeded once and reviewable as a report of its own, and every analysis that uses it joins the same values. It is also never written back into built, so built stays the data and the score stays a result computed from a named version of it, which is what lets join_artifact() refuse a stale one.

Is vars going away?

No. The function stays, and it is still the one place a study defines its analysis variables. What goes is the 900-line copy: the corrections move to the overlay, the deletions to the cohort, the models to their own jobs, and the umbrella blocks to rule rows. What is left is short enough to read, and each line is an action that can be tested.

My study came from SAS, and its data already has age_ln

This is the case to think about first, because every legacy study already in R is in it. bd.SAStoR.sas ran %vars before writing the XPORT file, so the dataset already carries the SAS transforms, flags and recodes. When the study is adopted (B0), the adoption job records that SAS applied vars, and records the SAStoR keep list as the study’s first variable set.

Then every primitive is idempotent, or refuses. If the column it would write already exists, it compares its own values with the ones there. If they agree, it does nothing more. If they do not, it stops and names the column. So running the R vars() over an adopted dataset can never silently transform twice, or quietly replace SAS’s definition of age_ln with a different one. A disagreement is a finding to look at, and it often turns out to be exactly the kind of copy-paste defect described at the top of this article.

How close is “agree” is still open: exact equality, or a tolerance for floating-point transforms that went through XPORT.

What is still open

These are decided later, and this article will follow the spec when they are:

  • how a job skips actions it does not need (above);
  • the match job’s prefix, since cm is already Cox matching in the taxonomy;
  • the rules repository’s name, its path under /programs/development/, and who reviews rule rows;
  • whether a dt job takes over bd’s diagnostic output, or bd’s report keeps it;
  • the idempotence tolerance for adopted data;
  • whether si, single imputation, survives once screening fill is a function and multiple imputation a job.

A census of the bd, vars and SAStoR programs across the corpus is staged and not yet run. Its counts may move an action from one row of the tables above to another.
